workload: ICC-profile image transforms (RGB to Lab, RGB to CMYK, CMYK to RGB, CMYK to CMYK, RGB soft-proof through CMYK, matrix-shaper RGB to RGB), 1 megapixel real photographs, GRACoL2006 and AdobeRGB1998 profiles, single thread, each measurement in its own process.
claimed_speedup: WASM SIMD kernels vs lcms-wasm 3.1-3.6x on every LUT workflow; vs native C lcms2 2.18: RGB to Lab 120.3 MPx/s (1.8x), RGB to CMYK 119.3 (1.9x), CMYK to RGB 78.6 (2.0x), CMYK to CMYK 80.8 (2.2x), soft-proof 115.9 (2.1x); matrix-shaper row 0.71x (native C faster) before the 1.5.5 fused matrix path, which the README says reaches 328 MPx/s vs 119 for the LUT path.
tradeoffs: Pure JavaScript, no native bindings; image path uses a baked CLUT so it is slightly less accurate than lcms2 (README: 100% of samples within 1 LSB of the LittleCMS oracle on the four tested workflows). JS/WASM only, not callable from C++.
caveats: Author states the native-C numbers come from the original 'steelman' harness and are being re-measured after feedback from the Little CMS author about incorrect lcms API calls (issue #6), so the vs-native-C column is provisional; the vs lcms-wasm figures are stated as unaffected. Reproduction script is public (node bench/reproduce.js) but was not opened. Single machine, first-party. Capped at C because of the open re-measurement.
found_via: WebSearch: ICC color management transform faster than Little CMS lcms2 SIMD benchmark open source

name: KLERP / KNERP
baseline: OpenCV resize (bilinear and nearest-neighbor interpolation)
workload: Grayscale (8-bit, single channel) image resize with bilinear (KLERP) and nearest-neighbor (KNERP) interpolation, up- and downscaling, AVX2 plus multithreading, matching OpenCV output.
claimed_speedup: README: 'exceeding OpenCV's implementation in speed by 25-100% while matching its output and capabilities in both interpolation modes'; 'the magnitude of the speed gain depends on whether you're downscaling or upscaling and by how much'. No per-case numbers are given.
compiler_and_flags: Repo Makefile (not stated as the flags used for the OpenCV comparison): g++ -Ofast -std=gnu++14 -mavx2 -march=native -mfma -flto -funroll-all-loops -fpeel-loops -ftracer -ftree-vectorize, -lpthread
tradeoffs: Single header KLERP.h with no dependencies. Needs an AVX2 CPU, uses its own threads (links pthread), and handles grayscale images only (the README says it is meant for computer vision). A CUDA sibling (CUDALERP, CUDAFLERP) by the same author covers GPU use.
caveats: Only the percentage range appears in the README. The driver main.cpp times KLERP alone (a 2x2 image upscaled to 800x2000) and does not run OpenCV, so the comparison cannot be reproduced from the repo. CPU, OpenCV version and OpenCV build options are not stated. main.cpp is dated Dec 26, 2016, so the OpenCV compared against is probably 3.x; OpenCV has since reworked resize with wide intrinsics, so the lead may have shrunk or vanished. Unclear whether the multithreaded KLERP was compared with single-threaded OpenCV.

name: LibGaussianBlur (FFT Gaussian blur, from Blur_algorithms)
baseline: OpenCV cv::GaussianBlur
workload: True Gaussian blur of RGB 24-bit images with sigma = sqrt(width) (very large kernels), FFT convolution with pffft (1D, separable) versus cv::GaussianBlur, 46 image sizes from 1500x1000 to 24000x14500 (README text says 45 images up to 11400x7600), Apple M3 Pro 12 cores.
claimed_speedup: README of the archived predecessor Blur_algorithms: 'surprisingly fast is the 1D implementation in pffft compared to OpenCV that is the standard market reference', linear versus exponential growth with size. Timings in py/performance.ipynb (ms, pffft vs cv::GaussianBlur): 2000x1300 11.52 vs 107.43; 6500x4000 114.97 vs 1604.24; 12000x7300 433.94 vs 6317.43; 24000x14500 1728.56 vs 33509.56. Derived from page data: 9x to 20x lower time for every size except the smallest; at 1500x1000 OpenCV was faster (24.97 ms vs 32.05 ms).
hardware: Apple M3 Pro, 12 cores, 16 MB cache setting for PocketFFT
tradeoffs: C++20 library using FFT tiles and pffft (a bundled FFT library); pads images to FFT-friendly sizes, so more memory than direct convolution; Python wheels, WebAssembly and mobile builds provided. The FFT approach pays off only for large sigma; small kernels are the OpenCV regime.
caveats: The numbers live in the archived predecessor repo Blur_algorithms (hard-coded timing arrays in a notebook; that repo shows no license), not in LibGaussianBlur's own README. Compiler, flags, OpenCV version and OpenCV build (IPP, threads, ARM NEON) are not stated. sigma = sqrt(width) means kernels of hundreds of taps, which is the case where direct separable convolution is slowest; the result does not transfer to small sigma, and OpenCV won at the smallest size. Gaussian blur is a filtering kernel, not resampling or colour conversion, so the fit to this category is borderline. The README and the notebook disagree on the size range. Last commit is an automated coverage-badge commit.

PR 1276 is co-authored with an AI assistant, uses a custom harness (not criterion), states no CPU or rustc flags, and went through two rounds of self-correction (an O(n squared) cost in parley's single-Layout approach and a memory-retention asymmetry); its raw data sits in tools/text-spike/ of the flui repo and was not opened. flui issue 931 relays an unverified downstream report that floem found parley '93% slower on Arabic wrap' and says not to cite it as settled. name: ucstrcase
baseline: icu::UnicodeString::caseCompare (ICU4C); strcasecmp also timed
workload: Case-insensitive comparison of generated UTF-8 strings, generated ASCII strings and worst-case matching UTF-8 strings (README timing loop; sizes and iteration counts not stated).

The text's '5x-10x' headline is inconsistent with its own table (ratios from 4.1x to 23x). Only 8 commits, all on one day in July 2024. Category fit is poor: case-insensitive string comparison, not shaping, rasterization or layout; probably belongs with string or Unicode utilities.

baseline: Pillow PNG encoder and Pillow JPEG 2000 plugin (in Image-Compression-Benchmark); the README compares against the original HP JPEG-LS code, JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000
workload: Lossless compression and decompression of 585 CLIC2021 RGB 24-bit images (4.1 GB), single-threaded, total time and total size, using the CharLS-based pillow-jpls 1.3.2 plugin.
claimed_speedup: Image-Compression-Benchmark (CLIC2021, units not stated on page, presumably seconds): JPEG-LS compress 72.237 and decompress 66.567 vs JPEG2000 319.912 and 275.398 (about 4.4x and 4.1x faster, derived from page data) and vs PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 and 33.677 (4.6x faster compress but about 2x slower decompress); JPEG-LS total size 1931584595 vs JPEG2000 1992860964 and PNG 2003016524 bytes. hardware: Intel Core i7 12700H, 16GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10
tradeoffs: JPEG-LS (ISO/IEC 14495-1) is a lossless/near-lossless codec with low complexity; decode is about twice as slow as Pillow's PNG decode in the cited suite. README notes Hewlett Packard patents on JPEG-LS (licensed free for conformant implementations; some may have expired). No SIMD: speed comes from templates and traits.
caveats: Weak fit to the listed baselines: none of libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp or libavif is directly compared, and Pillow's PNG codec uses zlib rather than libpng. The suite measures a Python wrapper (pillow-jpls, which PyPI says is based on CharLS), so Python overhead is included. The README's own 'twice as fast as HP code' claim cites a page on imagecompression.info that was not opened and is dated. Compression ratio is behind JPEG XL, EMMA and NBLI; the 'HALIC fast' variant trades size for speed and failed to decompress one gray test image (zone_plate.pnm) in the benchmark.

The numbers come from prebuilt executables with no flags. The PNG baseline is Pillow's zlib-based codec, not libpng. On tiny images PNG decodes faster (Kodak: PNG optimize=False 0.484 s versus HALIC 0.615 s), so the decode win shows only on large images. The author's own README charts carry no numbers.

name: meshoptimizer (vertex codec used as a lossless float-image compressor)
baseline: OpenEXR ZIP compression (zlib), also compared with EXR PIZ, RLE, HTJ2K and libjxl lossless
workload: Lossless compression of 10 floating-point EXR images (3122 MB total, half and float, up to 37 channels), split into 16K-pixel chunks compressed in parallel; compression ratio versus GB/s, 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: The author's conclusion: 'mesh optimizer is very impressive ... very far ahead of others towards top right of the chart'. Approximate readings of the Ryzen 5950X chart: decompression about 8 GB/s versus about 2.4 GB/s for EXR ZIP (about 3.3x, derived) at compression ratios of about 1.9 to 2.03 versus 1.87 for ZIP; compression about 1.3 to 1.8 GB/s versus about 1.2 GB/s for ZIP. JPEG-XL and HTJ2K are slower; the README says EXR HTJ2K decompresses at 2x slower than ZIP.
compiler_and_flags: Release cmake builds: Visual Studio 2022 v17.14 on Windows, Xcode clang 16 on Mac; OpenEXR 3.4.0, libjxl pre-v0.12 (029cec4), meshoptimizer v0.25, zstd 1.5.7 fetched via FetchContent

tradeoffs: Not an image format: the benchmark wraps meshoptimizer's vertex-data compression (vertex size set to the pixel size, padded to a multiple of four) in a custom chunked container written by the benchmark author, so there is no interoperability. Code size +26 KB (+431 KB with zstd) versus +308 KB for EXR HTJ2K and +6017 KB for JPEG-XL.

baseline: OpenJPEG (JPEG 2000 Part 1)
workload: Single-image decode time in the dicom-codecs shootout on three DICOM test images (8-bit color US, 12-bit gray MR, 16-bit gray CT); each codec decodes its own encoded stream, one iteration.

name: gif_load
baseline: giflib 5.2.2 (also stb_image)
workload: Wall-time decode of every frame of 6 synthetic animated GIFs (320x240 x100, 640x480 x200, 1920x1080 x150; flat shapes and incompressible noise), file read into RAM with read() or mmap(), cold and warm page cache.
claimed_speedup: Warm cache: 1.3x-1.7x faster than giflib and 1.4x-2.5x faster than stb_image (e.g. 1080p shapes 668 ms vs giflib stream 1149 ms vs stb_image 1829 ms). Cold cache: 1.3x-1.5x vs giflib on the 3 shape GIFs but 0.83x-0.85x (slower) on the 3 noise GIFs. Author says the 1.3x-1.5x cold claim also holds on real giphy GIFs. Peak memory: one frame plus a 16 KB code table versus giflib slurp 296 MB at 1080p.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5 -O2, Linux 6.4
hardware: CPU model not stated (RAM latency 128 ns, 8 GB/s sequential read, EXT4 cold disk read 342 MB/s)
tradeoffs: Whole file must be in memory before decoding (cannot overlap I/O with decode, which is why cold noise cases lose to giflib). Callback API, header-only, under 300 lines, no libc dependency apart from realloc. Interlaced GIFs are the caller's job to unwind (giflib's DGifSlurp does it). Public-domain dedication (no patent grant).
